text:
A Schedule Just Runs a Skill

Nothing new to learn. A schedule opens the same book from your library — just on a timer instead of you typing the trigger.



Skill = what to do. Schedule = when to do it, without you.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
section: The Problem with a Blank Prompt
text:
The Problem with a Blank Prompt

Earlier today: the brain has amnesia — it only knows what’s on the desk.



So put the right sources on the desk — and make it answer from those only.









The goal


Without grounding in real sources, even the smartest brain will guess.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Wrong Way vs. Right Way



Wrong
“Summarize the literature on active learning.”
→ Generic, maybe fabricated citations.



Right
Upload 5 papers → “Based only on these, summarize…”
→ Specific, citable, defensible.




No upload = no trust. Context comes before content.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
The Golden Rule

If it doesn’t have a citation, it didn’t happen.



For research, teaching materials, and committee work — demand the page reference.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
What It’s Best At

Deep reading of big documents (50+ pages). It builds a guide solely from your uploaded sources — no internet guessing — and every answer links back to the source.



Upload papers, a thesis, a policy, lecture readings
Ask questions; get answers with citations to the exact passage
Generate an Audio Overview to listen on your commute

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
NotebookLM Now Builds Slides

Turn your sources into a presentation — grounded in the same documents.





Detailed Deck
Text-rich, stands on its own. Good for a reading or handout.



Presenter Slides
Clean and visual — supports you while you talk.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Steering & Editing the Deck

Before generating: name your audience, emphasize themes, or structure it around specific questions
Export straight to .pptx — editable PowerPoint
Revise any slide: a pencil icon → type how to change the wording, emphasis, or visual








One requirement


You need at least one source uploaded before it can build a deck — grounding first, always.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Your Mission

Take a real (safe) paper or policy PDF. Produce a 1-page grounded summary and a presenter deck — in 10 minutes.



Upload the source to NotebookLM
Interrogate: “Based only on this, give 5 key findings with page references. If it’s not in the source, say ‘Not found.’”
Verify the citations — click through to the passage
Generate a Presenter deck → export .pptx → revise one slide




No source? Use one of your own — or sample_paper.md (links to open-access papers & policies).







Log it


10 minutes vs. the hours it used to take. That’s the number for the Wrap-up.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Quiz
1. You need to summarize a confidential, unpublished manuscript you’re reviewing.



Newspaper Test first. Confidential peer review — check the rules before uploading anywhere.




2. You need today’s statistics on enrollment trends from the web.




Deep Research — live web with citations. NotebookLM only reads your uploads.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Key Takeaways

Context before content — never start from a blank prompt
Grounding builds trust — upload sources, constrain to “only these”
No citation = didn’t happen — demand page references
NotebookLM — deep reading and decks (Detailed vs. Presenter, .pptx)
Right tool, right job — Cowork / NotebookLM / Deep Research

title: From Chat to Cowork
text:
Why Cowork?

Claude Cowork is the fastest way to turn AI into an assistant that works on your actual files — not just a chat tab.








Portable idea


Other tools have their own version of this. We use Cowork because the setup is the simplest — the concepts move with you.

title: From Chat to Cowork
text:
Chat vs. Assistant




A Chat Box

You paste, it replies
One message at a time
Closes → forgets






Cowork (an Agent)

Opens your files
Runs steps in order
Can act, not just talk






Same brain in the jar. A much more capable office around it.

title: From Chat to Cowork
text:
Three Steps to Running

Install the Claude desktop app and sign in
Open Cowork and point it at a folder on your computer
Type a task in plain language — and approve what it proposes



That’s it. No setup files, no code, no configuration.

title: From Chat to Cowork
text:
Meet the Working Directory

When Cowork opens, it points at one folder on your computer — its working directory.



“So that’s the office the two layers talked about.”



This folder is the office. Your context lives here as real, openable files.

Before letting it act, ask: “What’s the worst it could do if it’s wrong — can I undo it, and who’d notice in time?”


(industry term: blast radius)








Always start in draft / notify-me mode


Cowork proposes, you approve. Promote to act-on-its-own only after it has proven itself.

title: From Chat to Cowork
text:
The Staging Rule

Always work on copies of your files in a staging folder.



A mistake can’t touch your originals or a real grade sheet or a real inbox while you’re learning.

text:
Act Now or Propose & Wait?
1. “Reformat these notes into a clean summary in a new file.”



Act now — low blast radius, easy to undo.




2. “Email the revised grades to all 60 students.”




Propose & wait — irreversible, high blast radius. Review first.

text:

What is the working directory?




Your office — your context as real, openable files on your computer. Not a chat history.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
Hand It the Keys

So far the office gathers pages from your folder. But some pages you need live elsewhere — your inbox, calendar, or drive. A connector hands the agent the keys to those, so it can fetch and act, not just talk.



This is where AI stops being a chat box and starts touching your real work.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
What Changes

Cowork can now pull live information — today’s emails, this week’s calendar — and re-send it to the brain.



Same office loop. Wider reach.




(MCP is the technical “doorway standard” so any tool can offer a door the office knows how to open — the acronym is optional. Plugins bundle skills + connectors for a role.)

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
A Faculty Example

Connect your Drive and Calendar, then ask: “Read this week’s committee files from Drive and my calendar, and draft a week-ahead teaching summary.”



Now it pulls real documents and real dates — instead of you copy-pasting them in.









Keys earn trust slowly


Start read-only / draft-only: let it fetch and propose, never send or delete, until it has earned act-on-its-own.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
section: Keys Mean a Bigger Blast Radius
text:
Keys Mean a Bigger Blast Radius






Start in draft / notify-me mode


The moment the agent can reach a real inbox or drive, it can act outside your staging folder, in your real work. The undo test now has teeth — give it read-only or propose-only access first; promote to act-on-its-own only after it has earned your trust.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
Putting It All Together

Connector + Skill + Schedule, in draft mode:



“Every Monday, read my inbox (connector), summarize action items (skill), save to my folder, and notify me (schedule, draft mode).”




The whole toolkit, working as one teammate.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
Adding a Connector Changes…

What does adding an email connector change most?




The blast radius — what Cowork can now reach and act on. That’s exactly why it stays in draft / notify-me until it earns trust.

title: Connectors: Reaching Into Other Buildings
text:
Key Takeaways

Cowork ≠ chat — it opens files, runs steps, and can act; the working directory is the office
Second safety rule — the undo test / human-in-the-loop (blast radius); work on staging copies
Skill — a book Cowork opens by its trigger; it can bundle a script + a template
Script — code it writes & runs to compute exactly; Template — the on-brand layout the script fills
Schedule runs a skill on a clock; Connectors give it keys to your real tools — guardrails first: every job starts in draft / notify-me

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Two Layers, Stacked




The Model Layer
“The brain in a jar”





The App Layer
“The office around the brain”





Tell these apart and every “memory”, “Projects”, and “Skills” feature stops being magic.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
A Brilliant Brain — With Amnesia

A brilliant graduate’s brain floating in a jar. It has read most of the internet, so it keeps that knowledge — but it has amnesia about new information, so it will not know you.



Keeps its training: language, facts, math, reasoning — it stays genuinely smart
Has no memory of you: your work, your name, what you said five minutes ago
The instant it finishes answering, it forgets this conversation — not its skills




Two different things: the knowledge stays, the memory of you resets.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
section: It Predicts the Next Word — On Repeat
text:
It Predicts the Next Word — On Repeat
Under the hood it does one thing, over and over: pick the next word, append it, ask again. At each step, it’s choosing from a vocabulary of 256,000+ words and symbols.


“The capital of Saudi Arabia ___”

is (97%)
was (2%)
remains (0.6%)
all other words … (0.2%)



“The capital of Saudi Arabia is ___”

Riyadh (99%)
Jeddah (0.4%)
Mecca (0.3%)
all other words … (0.2%)



“The capital of Saudi Arabia is Riyadh ___”

, (52%)
. (41%)
: (4%)
all other words … (2%)



“The capital of Saudi Arabia is Riyadh, a ___”

city (61%)
large (12%)
major (8%)
all other words … (6%)





It doesn’t “know” geography — at each step it knows which word usually comes next, picks it, and repeats.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
When It Guesses Wrong (Hallucinations)

What happens when it doesn’t know the answer? It guesses.

“According to Article 214 of the new Investment Law: …”



The (45%) · Foreign (30%) · Capital (15%)





It constructs a sentence that sounds right, but it has never read the actual document. That confident, made-up answer is a hallucination.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Limit That Explains Everything

The model is stateless. It does not “remember” and it does not “look things up”.



Anything you want it to “know”, you must hand it every single time.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
We Build an Office

The brain in a jar can’t open files or remember your name. So we build an office around it: filing cabinets, a notebook, a standing to-do list.


Every time you ask for something, the office gathers the relevant pages and hands them to the brain along with your request — then files the answer back.



The brain still has amnesia. The office is what makes it feel like it remembers.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
What It Really Is

The app (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, an agent…) is the software wrapped around the model.


It stores your information in files / a directory and re-sends the relevant parts on every request.








The features you’ve seen


“Memory”, “Projects”, “Custom Instructions” are all just the app doing this gathering-and-resending for you.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Sentence to Remember

The model stays smart but remembers nothing about you; the app re-sends what matters on every request.



Every “smart” feature is just the app getting smarter about what to re-send.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Context = the Desk

Context is everything the office stacks on the brain’s desk before it starts — your request plus the background pages it needs to do the job well.


Your instructions, pasted documents, standing rules, relevant memory — the model’s entire world for that one request.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Big Reframe

Output quality is mostly a context problem, not a smartness problem.








What this means for you


A weak answer usually means weak context, not a weak model. “Give it context” is the whole skill.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Why Long Chats “Forget”

The brain’s desk has a fixed size. You can only fit so many pages on it at once. Pile on too much and older pages fall off the edge.



That’s the context window — and it’s why a long conversation starts losing the thread from the beginning.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Saved Beats Re-Pasted






The rule


Saved instructions beat re-pasting.



The app puts the important pages back on the desk for you every time, so they never fall off the edge.


This is the whole reason standing instructions, projects, and memory exist.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Office Getting Smarter
Everything you’ll build today is just the app deciding what to re-send:

Standing instructions — your rules, re-sent every time
Memory — facts about you, re-sent when relevant
Skill — a book in the library the app opens on command
Grounding — your sources put on the desk, on purpose



None of it is magic. It’s all context management.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Micro-Check
The AI cites a journal article that doesn’t exist. Which layer failed?



Both — and that’s the point. The brain guessed (model layer) because no real source was on its desk (context). Fix it the context way: ground it in a real source, then verify (later, with NotebookLM).

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Paradigm Shift

Stop chatting. Start delegating.



You don’t need a “chat bot”. You need a direct report — someone you brief properly, then trust to deliver.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Framework


R — Role: name the expert you’d hire — it shapes the AI’s vocabulary and priorities.


I — Instructions: what to do, bundled with its format, length, and tone.


C — Context: the raw material — paste your notes, upload your docs.


E — Examples: paste one sample of “good”; the AI copies its shape.









C is the same context from the two layers


You’re loading the pages onto the brain’s desk. No context = the brain guesses.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Formula

“Act as a [Role]. Your job is to [Instructions]. Here is the [Context]. Match this [Example].”



Examples are the secret weapon — one good sample teaches more than ten lines of rules.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Don’t Ask — Delegate

Don’t ask: “Write an email about the meeting.”



Delegate: “Act as a thesis advisor. Draft a recap email to my student from these notes. Highlight the revisions due before the next committee.”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Messy Notes

What you actually scribbled after the committee meeting:


“Met Sara re: thesis ch.3. Stats section weak — needs effect sizes, not just p-values. Lit review missing 2 key papers (ask her to add). Committee wants revised draft in 3 weeks. She’s nervous about the defense — reassure. Reminder: ethics form still not submitted.”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The RICE Prompt

Role: Act as a supportive thesis advisor.
Instructions: Draft a warm, clear follow-up email to my student. Use headers — Summary, Required Revisions, Deadline, Admin. Put the deadline in bold. End on an encouraging note. If anything is missing, add a “Questions for me” section.
Context: Notes from today’s committee meeting on Chapter 3: [paste notes]
Example: Match this opening — “Dear Sara, good progress this week. Here’s where we landed: …”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
What Made It Work

Role → wrote as a mentor, not a robot
Instructions → clear sections + tone + the “Questions for me” rule
Context → messy notes were enough — the AI extracted the structure
Example → matched the warm, personal opening

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Think Step by Step

Add “think step by step” so the AI reasons before it answers — best for logic, planning, and scheduling.


“8 chapters, 10 teaching weeks, midterm in week 6, chapters 5–6 must come before it — lay out a week-by-week plan. Think step by step.” → it sequences instead of guessing.



Chain of Thought. Often automatic now — reasoning models do this internally — but still worth asking simpler models, or when you want the steps shown.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Debate It Out

Make the AI argue from several expert viewpoints, then synthesize — best for judgment calls.


“A borderline thesis — one reviewer says pass, one says revise. Argue it as a strict methodologist, a supportive mentor, and an external examiner, then recommend one call.”



Tree of Thoughts.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Double-Check

Run the same prompt a few times and go with the answer that keeps coming up — best for judgment calls you can’t easily verify.


“Judge whether this paragraph’s argument is original or derivative — 3 separate times. Go with the verdict that repeats.”



Not for exact numbers. To total a column of scores, re-rolling still guesses — a script computes it exactly, every time. (That’s Session 2.)


Self-Consistency.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Quiz
You prompt: “Write feedback on this essay.” Which RICE elements are missing?





R — Role
Who’s giving it?



I — Instructions
Length? tone? rubric?



C — Context
The essay? the rubric?



E — Example
No sample of good feedback

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Key Takeaways

Two layers — the model (brain) and the app (office) stacked together
The brain keeps its training but forgets you — stateless, predicts the next word, can hallucinate
Quality is a context problem — the right pages on the desk → the right answer
Delegate, don’t ask — brief the AI with RICE (Role, Instructions, Context, Examples)
Examples are the secret weapon; slow it down on hard calls — step by step, debate it out, double-check (and use a script for exact numbers)

title: Practice — Delegate a Real Task
text:
Pick a “Messy → Clean” Task






Build


Pick one recurring “messy input → clean output” task and write a full RICE prompt:

Role — who should the AI be? (a supportive advisor, a peer reviewer…)
Instructions — the task + format, length, tone
Context — paste the real notes / rubric / draft
Example — one sample of the output you want






Starter ideas: meeting notes → student email · raw findings → abstract · reading → 1-page brief · rubric + essay → feedback note









Stuck for a task? Use our sample data



committee_notes.md → draft a committee-report email
sample_essay.md + rubric.md → write a feedback note
grades.csv → double-check exam totals

title: Practice — Delegate a Real Task
text:
Run It, Then Tighten It

Run the prompt — does the output match your Example?
Missing something? Add the one RICE element that’s weakest and re-run
Add the pro move: “If anything is unclear, ask me before you write.”



One good prompt you can reuse beats ten throwaway chats.

title: Practice — Delegate a Real Task
text:
Add the Matching Advanced Move






Build


Pick a calculation or judgment task and add the move that fits:

Numbers / totals → double-check (solve it 2–3 times; match = trust)
Logic / multi-step → “think step by step”
A close judgment call → “debate it out” (argue both sides first)






“Total these exam scores three times. If all three match, output ‘Verified’; if not, ‘Manual Review Needed’.”









Note


Sample data to practice on: grades.csv

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
The Problem

You retype the same multi-step request every time you need it — re-explaining the steps, the format, the style, from scratch.



There’s a better way: name it once, and run it with a single phrase.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
What a Skill Is

Your Skills are a library. Each Skill is a book — a written playbook for one recurring task.



Cowork keeps the whole shelf, but only opens the book your task calls for — not every book, every time. (just like the office puts only the relevant page on the desk)




The title on the spine — the trigger that tells Cowork which book to pull
What’s written inside — the steps, in plain language

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Skill vs. Just a Prompt



A prompt
Retyped from scratch every single time you need the task.




A Skill
That same prompt — named, saved, and bundled with its steps. One phrase runs it.





A Skill is a good prompt that stopped being disposable.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Demo 1 — “Lecture Deck” (revealjs)

Lecture notes → an on-brand revealjs slide deck you open in your browser.



Name: Lecture Deck  •  Trigger: “turn these notes into a revealjs deck”
Steps: 1) outline the storyline · 2) one idea per slide · 3) apply my course style · 4) generate a revealjs file with a Quarto front-matter

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Invoke It on Fresh Input

Skill saved — now just type the trigger on any new lecture:


“Turn this into a lecture deck: photosynthesis — light reactions, Calvin cycle, limiting factors, today’s lab.”



One phrase → a browser-ready deck. No re-explaining.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
What a Script Is

A little program Cowork writes and runs when the job is exact, repeatable calculation — math and data done the same way every single time.



The brain in a jar estimates — and can slip on arithmetic. A computer computes the same way every time. So Cowork doesn’t do the math in its head — it writes a script.









You still never touch code


A Skill is instructions Cowork reads and follows; a script is code it runs to compute. You never write or even see it: you describe what you want, Cowork writes and runs the script, you get the result.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
section: Template — the Layout the Script Fills
text:
Template — the Layout the Script Fills

A template is a pre-made, on-brand layout — a slide deck or a spreadsheet — that the script populates, so every output looks consistent.



The script does the work (compute, fill in the numbers)
The template gives it a shape (your style, your branding)
Same template next time → same look, no reformatting

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Composition — Skills Bundle Scripts + Templates

A Skill isn’t just steps. It can call a script to compute and fill a template to look right — all behind one trigger.



“turn these notes into a lecture deck” → the Skill outlines the story → a script generates the file → into your deck template → a finished, on-brand deck.




One phrase in. A polished result out. That’s composition.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Demo 2 — Grade Summaries

You have a spreadsheet of raw scores. You want weighted finals, the class average, and a distribution — every term.



“From grades.csv, compute each student’s weighted total (midterm 25%, final 35%, project 25%, participation 15%), the class average, and a grade distribution. Save it as a new sheet.”







Note


Sample data: grades.csv

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Why a Script Here

Exact, every row — the script computes, it doesn’t estimate
Reproducible next time — same script, same method; no formula errors, no copy-paste
You get the result, not the code — describe it once, Cowork writes and runs it








Pair it with “double-check”


For anything you report, ask it to compute twice and compare before you trust the numbers.

title: Build It Once: Skills, Scripts & Templates
text:
Script or Just Answer?

When should Cowork write a script instead of just answering?




When the work is exact or repeated calculation — determinism, not guessing. The brain estimates; a script computes the same way every time.
